triage.name: Allergic conjunctivitis
triage.reason: Itchy watery red eyes with seasonal triggers; diagnosis is clinical from history and exam, with good look-alikes (viral, bacterial, dry eye).

review_issues: auto-repaired: workup: 'Allergy testing (skin prick or serum specific IgE)' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if Persistent or severe symptoms despite treatment, or need to confirm atopy)
auto-repaired: workup: 'Conjunctival scraping for eosinophils' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if Atypical presentation where diagnosis is unclear)
exam: term 'Circumcorneal injection' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Purulent discharge from eye' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: Common in children and young adults
Peaks in spring and fall for seasonal allergic conjunctivitis
More common in individuals with atopy

risk_factors.text: Personal history of allergic rhinitis, asthma, or atopic dermatitis
Exposure to animal dander or dust mites

hpi.onset: Acute, often within minutes to hours after exposure to an allergen; may be recurrent with seasonal pattern
hpi.duration: Days to weeks during allergen exposure, resolves with avoidance or treatment
hpi.progression: Bilateral watery, itchy, red eyes that may worsen with continued allergen exposure; often accompanied by sneezing and clear nasal discharge
hpi.timing: Worse during pollen season or after animal exposure; improves indoors with air conditioning
aggravating: Going outside during high pollen counts

argues_against: Unilateral eye pain with decreased vision
Purulent discharge with matting of lashes

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children may rub their eyes constantly and be irritable; they often have concurrent allergic rhinitis and eczema.
Older adults may have more burning and dryness due to coexistent dry eye, making itching less prominent.
Hormonal changes can worsen dry eye or cause nonspecific redness, so allergic conjunctivitis may be harder to distinguish.

general.moderate: Awake and comfortable; frequent eye rubbing and puffy eyelids
general.severe: Uncomfortable; constant tearing and swollen eyelids, but no systemic distress

findings.maneuver: Inspect the conjunctiva with a bright light, retract the lower lid
Inspect the tear film and lid margin
Evert the upper eyelid and inspect the tarsal conjunctiva
findings.finding: Cobblestone papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva

findings.maneuver: Inspect the limbal area with a penlight or slit lamp
Inspect the discharge and lid margins
Stain the cornea with fluorescein and examine under cobalt blue light

imaging.preferred_when: Only if there is concern for orbital cellulitis, proptosis, or painful ophthalmoplegia

findings.text: No orbital inflammation, abscess, or sinus disease

supporting.test: Allergy testing (skin prick or serum specific IgE)
supporting.only_if: Persistent or severe symptoms despite treatment, or need to confirm atopy

supporting.why: Eosinophils on Giemsa stain support allergy
supporting.only_if: Atypical presentation where diagnosis is unclear

not_indicated.why: Blood counts are normal and do not help diagnose allergic conjunctivitis
Only if orbital cellulitis is suspected; not for routine allergic conjunctivitis
Not needed unless purulent discharge suggests bacterial infection

decision_points: Reserve cultures and imaging for signs of severe infection (purulent discharge, preauricular adenopathy, proptosis, vision loss)
Allergy testing is outpatient and not part of acute diagnosis

criteria.name: Clinical diagnosis of allergic conjunctivitis
criteria.summary: Diagnosis is based on bilateral itching, watery discharge, conjunctival hyperemia, and often a history of atopy or allergen exposure; absence of purulent discharge, significant pain, vision changes, or preauricular lymphadenopathy.
items: History of atopy or allergen exposure
No purulent discharge, preauricular adenopathy, or vision loss

differential.name: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
differential.why_considered: Acute red eye with pain and decreased vision; must not miss among causes of red eye
differential.trigger: Unilateral severe eye pain with headache, nausea, vomiting, or halos around lights

history: Sudden severe unilateral eye pain
Blurred vision or halos around lights
Headache, nausea, or vomiting
Often older adult, hyperopic, or dim light trigger
exam: Conjunctival injection most marked at the limbus (ciliary flush)
Shallow anterior chamber on slit lamp

differential.name: Infectious keratitis
differential.why_considered: Painful red eye with photophobia and decreased vision, especially in contact lens wearers
differential.trigger: Contact lens wearer with eye pain, photophobia, or corneal opacity

history: Unilateral eye pain or foreign body sensation
Photophobia
Blurred vision
Contact lens use
exam: Corneal infiltrate or ulcer on fluorescein staining
labs: Corneal scrapings for culture if bacterial or fungal keratitis suspected

differential.name: Viral conjunctivitis
differential.why_considered: Red watery eyes with mild itching or burning; common cause of red eye

history: Often starts in one eye then spreads to the other
Recent upper respiratory infection or sick contacts
Watery discharge
Mild to moderate itching, less prominent than in allergic conjunctivitis
exam: Follicular conjunctival reaction on tarsal conjunctiva

differential.name: Bacterial conjunctivitis
differential.why_considered: Red eyes with discharge; need to distinguish purulent from watery discharge

history: Purulent discharge, eyelids matted in morning
Usually starts in one eye then may spread
Less itching than allergic conjunctivitis
exam: No preauricular lymphadenopathy except in hyperacute gonococcal cases
labs: Conjunctival swab culture only if severe or hyperacute

differential.name: Dry eye syndrome
differential.why_considered: Chronic red, irritated eyes; can cause bilateral redness, tearing, and mild itching

history: Burning or gritty sensation rather than itch
Worse with prolonged screen use or low humidity
Symptoms often worse at end of day
exam: Punctate epithelial erosions on fluorescein staining
labs: Schirmer test may show decreased tear production

differential.name: Blepharitis
differential.why_considered: Bilateral red, irritated eyes with eyelid involvement; can have itching and tearing

history: Chronic crusting on lashes
Burning sensation, worse in morning
Recurrent symptoms
exam: Collarettes or scaling at base of lashes

severity.mild: Mild intermittent itching and redness, no eyelid edema or chemosis, resolves with allergen avoidance or over-the-counter antihistamine eye drops
severity.moderate: Persistent symptoms with eyelid edema, chemosis, or papillary reaction; interferes with daily activities but no vision change; requires prescription topical antihistamine/mast cell stabilizer or short-term topical corticosteroid
severity.severe: Intense symptoms with marked eyelid edema, chemosis, or severe papillary conjunctivitis; may be refractory to usual topical treatment; requires ophthalmology referral and possibly topical corticosteroids under supervision

red_flags.meaning: Consider keratitis, uveitis, or acute angle-closure glaucoma
Viral conjunctivitis or hyperacute bacterial conjunctivitis

red_flags.finding: Corneal opacity or infiltrate on fluorescein staining
red_flags.meaning: Corneal ulcer or keratitis; needs urgent ophthalmology evaluation

red_flags.finding: Ciliary flush, hazy cornea, or fixed mid-dilated pupil
red_flags.meaning: Acute angle-closure glaucoma until proven otherwise

complications.name: Keratoconus from chronic eye rubbing
clues: History of chronic vigorous eye rubbing

complications.name: Secondary bacterial conjunctivitis
clues: Change from watery to purulent discharge

complications.name: Steroid-induced glaucoma or cataract
clues: History of prolonged topical corticosteroid use

special_populations.differences: Often accompanied by allergic rhinitis and eczema; may rub eyes constantly; diagnosis is clinical, and topical antihistamines/mast cell stabilizers are first-line
Itching may be less prominent and coexistent dry eye may blur the picture; burning and dryness may dominate
Hormonal changes can aggravate dry eye and nonspecific redness, making diagnosis harder; prefer topical therapy with minimal systemic absorption

key_questions.question: When did your eye symptoms start, and were both eyes affected at the same time?
key_questions.looking_for: Rapid onset of bilateral symptoms after allergen exposure

key_questions.question: Do your eyes itch?
key_questions.looking_for: Prominent itching; this is the cardinal symptom of allergic conjunctivitis

key_questions.question: Is there any discharge? Can you describe it?
key_questions.looking_for: Clear and watery discharge, not purulent or mucoid

key_questions.question: Do you have sneezing, a runny nose, or stuffy nose?
Any eye pain or sensitivity to light?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; severe pain or photophobia suggests keratitis, uveitis, or angle-closure glaucoma

key_questions.question: Has your vision changed in either eye?
key_questions.looking_for: No decrease in vision; visual change requires urgent evaluation

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any swelling in front of your ears or in your neck?
key_questions.looking_for: Absence of preauricular lymphadenopathy; its presence suggests viral or hyperacute bacterial conjunctivitis

key_questions.question: Do you have a history of eczema, asthma, or seasonal allergies?
key_questions.looking_for: Personal atopy, which supports the diagnosis

key_questions.question: Have you been around pets, pollen, dust, or new eye products?
Do you wear contact lenses?
key_questions.looking_for: Contact lens wear marks a red flag for infectious keratitis; if present, do not dismiss as simple allergy

key_questions.question: What eye drops or medications have you tried? Did anything help?
key_questions.looking_for: Improvement with antihistamine or mast-cell-stabilizer drops; no frequent topical vasoconstrictor use

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have allergies, asthma, or eczema?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of atopy raises prior probability

reasoning_points: Bilateral itching is the hallmark of allergic conjunctivitis.
Clear watery discharge rather than purulent discharge makes bacterial conjunctivitis less likely.
History of atopy or allergen exposure and associated allergic rhinitis support the diagnosis.
Eye exam shows conjunctival hyperemia and often eyelid edema or papillary reaction, with a clear cornea and normal vision.
Absence of ciliary flush, preauricular lymphadenopathy, pain, photophobia, and decreased vision helps exclude serious causes.
Diagnosis is clinical; allergy testing or conjunctival scraping are reserved for atypical or refractory cases.
Must not miss contact-lens-related infectious keratitis, acute angle-closure glaucoma, or hyperacute bacterial conjunctivitis.

easy: Bilateral itchy, watery, red eyes after grass or pet exposure
Clear discharge, normal vision, no preauricular lymphadenopathy
Also has sneezing and clear rhinorrhea
medium: Contact lens wearer with red, irritated eyes and mild discomfort
Older adult with burning, dryness, and only mild itch
Papillary reaction or eyelid edema requiring differentiation from viral conjunctivitis
Perennial symptoms with dust mite or mold exposure
hard: Contact lens wearer with unilateral pain, photophobia, and corneal infiltrate
Severe acute red eye with nausea, halos, and fixed mid-dilated pupil
Infant or young child who cannot describe itch and has recurrent eye rubbing
Refractory symptoms despite topical therapy, raising concern for alternative or mixed pathology
